One of the best things to build with Argon is a new version of old, boring SaaS.

Old SaaS is legacy software that businesses pay for, but nobody updated it in a long time. 

Thousands of these products charge money. Your version can be better and cost $0.

Here is the whole setup:

1) Find a recurring problem. Look on G2, Capterra, Idea Browser, and Reddit.

2) Read what people complain about in the old product. Put the fixes in yours.

3) Make it focused on one niche. Example: a commercial cleaning company that makes price quotes in a spreadsheet.

4) Give Argon the complaints, the source links, and the workflow. Tell it to explain its plan, build the app, and list what is unfinished. In my test, it made interactive margin calculators with one prompt.

5) Release it as a free tool.

6) Sell your second, third, and fourth tools to the same buyers.

Step 6 only works after step 5. People buy from you after they trust you.

Argon gets the engineering right on the first prompt. For a good design, give it references and work with it.

In the past, I was scared to vibe code a product. The deployment was not good or not secure. 

Frontier AI now makes software that works, and it is probably better than the product it replaces.

Since I have the @Dell Pro Max with GB300 on hand and was leaving town for 3 days, I figured I'd give it some real homework to chew on!

I tasked it with an iterative loop of trying to improve my Robotron AI.  The prompt told it to make its "best attempt" at improving the AI, then A/B test it with confidence, then repeat forever.

I came back three days later to find the primary score metric had jumped from 1,000,000 to 5,000,000, a 5X increase in ability!

The GB300 runs 192 copies of MAME, each running an instrumented copy of Robotron.  That's about 8000 frames per second of gameplay.  And it does it all on the GB300's CPU cores, with only half the CPU being used.

Of course, the star of the show is the Blackwell GPU, which handles the reinforcement-learning training.  While I was away, it trained on 2.6 B frames of Robotron gameplay.

Our "old" machine had dual RTX 6000s, so it was no slouch, but the GB300 smokes it!

It's not recursive self-improvement yet, but it's a pretty solid example of iterative self-improvement!

This might be the most underrated AI story of today.

According to CNBC, TikTok's US business is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, with one source suggesting the company is targeting 4 GW by the early 2030s. I don't think people understand how significant this is. We're talking about a social media platform potentially looking to secure enough power and computing infrastructure to rival some of the largest AI data center developments in the country. For perspective, Meta's massive Hyperion data center campus in Louisiana is targeting around 5 GW of capacity.

TikTok already relies primarily on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and the company has confirmed that $ORCL will remain its primary cloud provider in the United States. On top of that, TikTok is retraining its recommendation algorithm using American user data and is developing AI products focused on large model inference and creative automation. In other words, this isn't necessarily just about supporting people scrolling through videos anymore. TikTok could be preparing for significantly more AI workloads which would require enormous amounts of computing power.

Now connect this to everything else we've been discussing. Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and xAI are already competing to secure power, GPUs, land, and data center capacity. Now we're seeing another major technology platform potentially entering that same competition at the gigawatt scale. And remember, these companies cannot simply decide they want another gigawatt of computing capacity and have it available tomorrow. They need electricity, substations, cooling infrastructure, networking equipment, GPUs, memory, and facilities capable of supporting all of it.

This is exactly why I remain so bullish on the companies supplying the infrastructure behind AI. Whether we're talking about $NVDA, $MU, $ORCL, $BE, or the broader networking and power ecosystem, the number of potential customers competing for limited resources continues to grow. What's particularly interesting is that this demand is increasingly coming from companies outside the handful of frontier AI labs everyone focuses on. I think we're still underestimating just how much infrastructure the AI economy is going to need over the next decade.

Internal evaluations reportedly show substantial gains on SWE-bench and Deep SWE compared with earlier Barium-B checkpoints. One employee described it as feeling like “Opus 5.5,” while some employees had acknowledged that Gemini Argon still fell short in certain areas.

Reports suggest that internal A/B testing has expanded across testing environments, primarily AGY, though other environments may also be involved.

Carbon’s eventual release format remains unclear. It could replace Argon directly, become a separate performance tier within the Gemini 4 lineup, or serve as a final refinement of Argon that addresses its remaining weaknesses - including concerns from users who consider it “benchmaxxed.”

Carbon appears to belong to Gemini 4’s ongoing checkpoint development process, which uses element-based names such as Argon, Barium, and Carbon. Internal documents identified Barium-B as the build chosen for Argon’s public release. That leaves open the possibility that Carbon could become an upgraded checkpoint within Gemini 4.x, potentially serving as a polished, stable final version of Gemini 4 Argon. That’s my interpretation, though, rather than a confirmed plan.

Some community members expect Gemini 4 Flash to launch soon, possibly alongside Carbon. There have been hints of a Flash release, but, from what I’ve seen, there isn’t enough evidence to establish either that timing or a connection to Carbon.

Carbon reportedly runs two to four times slower than Argon, which could suggest a heavier reasoning model. My personal take is that Google may be positioning Carbon to compete for the top spot ahead of Fable 5.5. Another possibility is that a backup checkpoint developed into a much stronger candidate than expected following Argon’s release and successive improvements.

If those reported gains hold up, Carbon could address several weaknesses in Google’s current flagship, Gemini 4 Argon: greater reliability, stronger performance on long-running tasks involving multiple steps, and improvements in important benchmark areas where Argon trails. It might also deliver more cost-efficient task completion, although that remains speculative.

During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy.

The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server.

This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE.

        10月19日至23日，A股走出了先撑后跌、周五强势反弹的一周。周一沪指上涨0.39%，深成指上涨0.13%，创业板指却下跌0.94%，市场分化已经显露；随后几个交易日，科技成长板块持续承压，市场调整不断加深。到了周五，行情突然逆转，三大指数低开高走，沪指上涨0.89%，深成指上涨2.79%，创业板指大涨4.16%，两市成交额放大至约1.96万亿元，全市场超过4500只个股上涨。市场要见底了吗？
         这一周最重要的特征，不是周五涨了多少，而是市场在经历连续下跌后，终于出现了一次力度很强的反弹。但我要强调，单日大涨不等于趋势反转，周五的反弹也不能抹去此前市场暴露出来的风险。按周度数据看，沪指全周下跌0.69%，深成指下跌1.09%，创业板指下跌3.18%。这说明市场整体仍然承压，尤其是创业板代表的成长方向，弱势并没有因为周五一根大阳线就被彻底扭转。最重要的一点，看涨幅榜是超跌的科技故事会带动，低估值纹丝不动，这明显不是反转！
          回顾本周的市场表现，我此前反复强调的几个问题，已经越来越清楚。第一，科技概念的风险仍然是市场不能回避的问题。前期被资金反复炒作的算力硬件、人工智能相关概念，在调整中暴露出明显的脆弱性。10月22日，创业板指单日下跌4.37%，新易盛跌超12%，多只科技概念股大幅下挫。到了23日，科技成长板块又成为反弹的重要力量。这恰恰说明，当前资金博弈激烈，热点反转速度很快。对于缺乏业绩支撑、估值过高的概念股，我依然不认为一次暴涨就能证明风险解除。真正值得关注的，是企业有没有核心技术、真实订单和持续盈利能力，而不是股价能不能连续涨停。
        第二，低估值股票的价值修复依然值得期待，但不能把个别银行股创新高直接等同于市场全面走强。本周工商银行、建设银行再创历史新高，银行板块局部回暖，说明低估值方向仍有资金关注。然而，银行股的上涨究竟是价值修复，还是机构在关键时刻稳定指数，仍然需要后续走势来验证。我的观点一直很明确：低估值股票长期被忽视，价值修复不可能一日完成；但如果市场只有少数权重股支撑指数，大量个股却持续下跌，这样的行情就谈不上真正健康。
         第三，610天线已经成为下一阶段最重要的观察位置。本周沪指在下跌过程中触及610天线，随后出现回升。我一直重视这条长期均线，因为它是判断市场中长期趋势的重要参考。周五的强势反弹，给市场带来了一定喘息空间，但现在就宣布610天线已经确认见底，显然还为时过早。尤其科创50距离610还很远，而科创板估值最高，是必然打到610的！
         对于周五的反弹，我的判断是：这是一次有力度的反弹，但还构不成反转。真正决定后市方向的，不是某一天涨得有多猛，而是反弹能否延续，市场广度能否保持，如果继续靠科技故事会拉抬，那就是镰刀割多少韭菜的问题，市场必然再次回落。尤其周五美股下跌，如果下周A股反弹迅速衰减，并且持续走弱，那么周五的上涨就可能只是调整过程中的一次强力反抽。
           展望下周，我重点观察三个信号：一是沪指在610天线附近能否保持稳定，二是周五的放量上涨能否延续，三是上涨能否从少数热点扩散到更广泛的个股。如果这三个信号不能得到后续走势的支持，我仍然不会轻易认定市场已经反转。尤其是前期涨幅巨大、估值高企的科技概念，即使继续反弹，也不值得不加区分地追涨。
         从板块来说，未来一旦有行情，哪个板块机会最大？我觉得医药股里肯定会出大牛股，包括疫苗类，如果是动物疫苗还有宠物概念，潜力很大，电力股是长期看好的重头戏，毕竟有算电协同，算力估值太高我们不建议做，电力可以，再其次就是看战略小金属里有没有低估值品种，这个也有想象空间，但整体看这都是后话，首要任务要确定这后面是不是一个坑，别偷鸡不成蚀把米！
        本周市场给出的教训很清楚：下跌时不能盲目抄底，反弹时同样不能盲目追高。610天线的考验还没有结束，周五的反弹究竟是趋势转折的开始，还是下跌过程中的一次强力反抽，需要下周行情给出答案。在信号真正明朗之前，我宁愿建议耐心等待，也不会建议为了交易而交易。况且你们了解到的只是官方公布的好消息，经济走势的暗面你们一无所知，那里又黑又冷。。。。

台積電說封裝「有一點短缺」，同一週輝達跟封測廠再簽 24 億美元，連同 Amkor 先前的亞利桑那協議，有寫出金額的承諾合計 41 億美元。
荷蘭封裝設備商 Besi 這週交出第三季：訂單 3.426 億歐元，年增 96%，比市場預估多了一成五。
股價呢？從 6 月高點到現在，大約腰斬。
再往前一週，台積電法說。7 月魏哲家說，封裝緊到「已經在限制客戶成長」。10/15 被問到跟格芯的合作，他說後段「有一點短缺」。
所以很多人的結論是：封裝的戲演完了，CoWoS 不缺了。
我看完這兩週的公告，想法剛好反過來。缺口還在，只是有人先付了錢，把它排到後面幾年。
從「瓶頸」到「有一點」，中間發生什麼事
10/8，格芯公告跟台積電簽了 5 年、20 億美元的合約，在紐約 Malta 幫 CoWoS 做矽中介層，2028 年上半年開始放量。
 
中介層就是 GPU 跟 HBM 坐的那片矽板。台積電把最緊的那一段，分一塊給別人做。
魏哲家在法說會上被問到這筆合作，原話是：
"Definitely, we have a little bit shortage on the back end, and we'd like to work with our so-called partner with GlobalFoundries."
法說會上他也講了：5 倍光罩尺寸已經量產，良率很好；9 倍、14 倍在開發；客戶的首選還是 CoWoS。
板子越做越大，一片晶圓切得出來的中介層就越少。台積電找了人一起扛。
台積電自己也沒停。這次法說它說，全球有將近 20 座廠同時在推，未來幾年在台灣要蓋 13 座先進製程和先進封裝廠，海外另外 5 到 6 座。今年資本支出 600 到 640 億美元，10 月法說會上重申不變（7 月講過其中一到兩成給先進封裝、測試、光罩這些）。
一家說「只有一點短缺」的公司，同時在蓋十幾座廠，還把一段工作外包到紐約。我讀起來，是缺口大到自己蓋不夠快。
輝達這週付的是頭期款
10/21，輝達在 GTC Berlin 一口氣公布一串供應鏈合約：
Amkor：南韓再加 13 億美元，連同先前的亞利桑那，多年協議（含預付款）合計 30 億美元；南韓目標 2028 年底中介層晶圓產能增加超過 300%。
京元電：11 億美元「產能保留預付款」，蓋美國測試廠，2027 年 4 月量產。
載板：揖斐電、三星電機、欣興，三年內輝達可用的載板產能合計拉到 2.5 倍。
矽品：CPO 光引擎產能，2027 年中拉到 15 倍。
 

有寫出金額的加起來：Amkor 30 億＋京元電 11 億，41 億美元，其中這週新增的是 Amkor 南韓 13 億＋京元電 11 億＝24 億，Amkor 亞利桑那那段是之前就簽的。揖斐電那筆只寫「數十億美元」（今年稍早已公布），還沒算進去。
 
這就像搶預售屋。房子還是一張設計圖，你先把頭期款匯過去，建商才肯幫你留那一戶。
麻煩的是交屋日期。京元電美國廠 2027 年 4 月。欣興新產能 2027 年第二季才開始加，2028 年中才滿載。格芯 2028 上半年。Amkor 2028 年底。
 

黃仁勳在同一份新聞稿講得更直接：「需求非比尋常，產能才是限制。」
瓶頸搬去哪
第一站，載板。
Google TPU v9 裡聯發科設計的 HumuFish 改走英特爾 EMIB-T（博通設計的 WhaleFish 還是 CoWoS-L），大家說台積電 CoWoS 被搶單。但 KeyBanc 估，EMIB-T 載板良率揖斐電約 50–60%、欣興只有 20–30%。這是分析師估計，不是公司公布。
TrendForce 10/22 引述天下雜誌和業界消息，第三季 EMIB-T 載板良率約 35%（年底目標 50%），但供應鏈說 HumuFish 仍「100%」用 EMIB-T。
35% 是什麼意思？你要 100 片好板，得投將近 286 片下去。
 

英特爾拿到的是門票，產能還要等良率爬上來。
第二站，機台。
Besi 今年前九個月的混合鍵合訂單，已經是 2025 全年的兩倍以上，客戶 23 家，累計需求超過 215 台。
 
那股價為什麼腰斬？一個是 SemiAnalysis 說 ASML 可能在做對手機台（ASML 沒證實，Besi 執行長說 ASML 不是對手）；另一個是市場擔心記憶體廠 HBM 導入混合鍵合會比較慢（執行長在法說也承認導入「有點延後」，但說開發沒停）。
還有一個原因比較少人講：Besi 說第四季營收大概跟第三季持平，上下 5%。訂單已經進來，機台還沒出貨，營收要晚幾季才跟上。股價看下一季，訂單看明後年。
第三站，測試。 輝達自己說，測試產能 2026 到 2027 要翻倍。
接下來我會盯的三個數字
台積電下一次法說：「有一點短缺」會不會又變回「瓶頸」。
EMIB-T 載板良率，從 35% 爬到 50–60% 要多久。
Besi 第四季訂單：公司說訂單動能會延續到第四季。
非投資建議，只是我自己的研究筆記。（我持有欣興）

ASML is bringing lithography-grade precision to hybrid bonding.

《为什么中国的银行能走出独立于西方银行的行情？》

中国与海外看似都在政府加杠杆、财政扩张，为什么中国银行表现反而不错？答案不在景气度的高低，而在周期位置与政策投向的差异。日本的对照很能说明问题：日本银行同样面临浮亏问题，但其利率上升处于偏早期，浮亏对盈利仍是贡献，而欧美一些银行已处于周期中后期，这就是周期位置的不同。

具体到中国银行业，可以从三个角度理解：

第一，财政投向不同。 欧美市场一看到财政扩张、赤字加码，直接反应是通胀上升并抛售长期债券。中国的财政投向则更加多元：今年年初两会提出的13.9万亿元政府总融资计划中，约3万亿元与金融稳定相关，包括地方政府债务置换，也包括对金融机构3000亿元的注资。这些政策对金融机构资产负债表起到修复作用——也就是说，今年新增的13.9万亿元融资中约1/5是在做金融稳定，对银行的影响自然不同。

第二，利率周期不同。 欧美处于高利率环境的时间比中国更长，高利率可能带来信用成本、存款成本上升、债券浮亏等一系列问题。中国利率周期处于历史较低位置，且总体稳定、波动不大。一个关键数字是：据测算，最近几年银行其他非息收入对利润的贡献每年在1—2个百分点左右，其中相当一部分正是债券投资收益和债券浮盈兑现。同样的债券，在欧美利率环境下是拖累，在中国利率环境下却是利润贡献。

第三，信用周期不同。 衡量信用周期可用"信贷脉冲"这一指标，即以新增信贷或社融除以GDP，用以刻画金融周期位置。结论是：中国金融周期处于最近几年比较低的位置，而海外金融周期处于过去几年偏高的位置，信贷脉冲仍处扩张阶段。不良率同样反映信用周期位置——中国不良率约1.5%，处于历史偏低位置且非常稳定，今年整体基本持平；而海外利率环境较高，不良率可能逐渐上升，不确定性高于中国。

最后总结：

"东升西降"的实质并不是东方银行比西方银行更赚钱，而是同一个高利率环境在不同周期位置上产生了相反的效果：欧美银行已从高利率周期上半段进入中后段，息差扩张空间收窄、信用成本与存款成本开始上行、账面债券浮亏积累，而长端利率上行的背后还叠加了财政可持续性的长期担忧；中国银行则处于利率周期的低位、信用周期的低位，财政扩张中又有相当比例直接用于修复金融机构资产负债表，债券在资产端反而是利润来源。

因此，这一分化首先反映的是市场担忧点的转移：从"高利率利好银行盈利"，转向"高利率本身会成为风险来源"。它不代表长期的趋势性拐点，也不意味着海外银行即将集中爆雷；真正需要持续跟踪的，是利率将继续上行、在通胀高位长期停留，还是能够较快回落——因为高利率环境下，哪个环节会先出问题，往往只有在问题发生之后才能确认。

这也是我反复跟星球朋友说的，不要尝试预测系统性的流动性冲击，我们根本不知道在高利率环境下，哪个机构、行业、板块先爆雷。

Five Errors Per Million. A New Record.

Quantinuum just reported a logical error rate of 5 per million operations on its Helios machine.

That is 99.9995% logical fidelity, ten times better than its own record from September.

Before anyone panics: this does not break any encryption. It is a benchmark for reliable computation, not an attack. Quantinuum says it points toward Apollo, a fault-tolerant machine it is targeting for 2029.

Why it still matters. Long quantum attacks need reliable logical qubits, and error correction is the gap between today's noisy machines and ones that can run them. Earlier this year Google researchers estimated that fewer than 500,000 physical qubits could derive a private key from an exposed public key in about nine minutes.

Every result like this moves the date a little closer, and nobody knows which one is the last.

QuanChain does not bet on a date. Its oracle tracks the cost per logical qubit-hour, and wallets move to stronger security levels at their next spend. Value at rest sits behind an address hash, not an exposed public key.

The hardware is getting better. The design should not need a forecast.

Expert Takeaways: TSMC

1. CoWoS Capacity, Fab Breakdown, Spill‑Over Orders & Customer Allocation

Capacity Expansion: TSMC's internal CoWoS monthly capacity is targeted to reach 130k wafers by end-2026, with a long-term goal of 260k wafers/month by 2028 (excluding OSAT volumes).

Demand Growth: Market demand for CoWoS has increased by at least 26% compared to early-2026 levels.

Fab Breakdown: AP8 full capacity is 50k wafers (>40k expected by end-2026); AP7-P1 reached its 35k full-load target after ramping in August; AP7-P2 focuses primarily on SoIC; US AP1 will not ramp significantly by year-end; legacy AP1–AP6 fabs handle the remaining volume.

Expansion Bottlenecks: New packaging fab construction takes about three years from groundbreaking to bottleneck-limited full output, constrained mainly by hybrid bonding and 3–4 nm-grade CMP flatness requirements.

OSAT Spill-Over Strategy: Lower-margin orders are routed to external OSATs (ASE, SPIL, Amkor) under signed LTAs, reserving TSMC’s internal capacity for high-value customers.

Customer Allocation Split: Nvidia (60%), Broadcom (15%), AMD (10%), Marvell (6%), AWS in-house silicon (5%), MediaTek (2%), and others (3%).

2. SoIC Capacity Roadmap, Capital Intensity, Fab Bottlenecks & End‑Use Drivers

Capacity Roadmap: Targeted at 15k wafers/month by end-2026, 24–28k by end-2027, and up to 45k by end-2028 (~90% CAGR in 2027).

Capital Intensity & Bottlenecks: Capital intensity is $6.8–7.0 billion per 10k monthly wafers. Hybrid-bonding pick-and-place tools are the initial bottleneck, shifting dynamically to PVD and PECVD.

Manufacturing Limits: High CMP flatness and particle cleanliness requirements create a hardware ceiling below CoWoS scale. Capacity is concentrated at Chiayi AP7 through end-2027 (long-term potential 40–50k/month). US AP1 will take future volume but faces a long learning curve requiring Taiwan team transfer.

Key Demand Drivers: Nvidia (Rubin Ultra / Feynman), AMD (MI400 / Venice), Apple (M5 Pro / Max), and Broadcom ASICs slated for 2027.

3. Competitive Landscape (Intel / Samsung), Yields & Risk Mitigation

Intel EMIB-T Status: Yield estimates vary from ~90% (supply chain) to 38–40% (test-vehicle data). EMIB-T die cost is ~50% of CoWoS-L. Intel outsources all backend assembly to Amkor across Longtan, Portugal, and Arizona.

Samsung & Competitor Scale: Samsung I-Cube yield maturity lags peers, with meaningful competitive threats unlikely until post-2030 when hybrid bonding matures. Overall, TSMC’s advanced packaging volume is ~5× that of Intel.

Customer De-Risking: Google is validating EMIB-T as a backup due to TSMC tightness, costs, and US policy. Broadcom is evaluating EMIB-T and Samsung capacity, while building a joint substrate/FC-BGA facility in Singapore with Toppan.

4. CoPoS Technical Bottlenecks, Production Timeline & Silicon Utilization

Realistic Timeline: Mass CoPoS production in 2027–2028 is overly optimistic. AP7 has started qualification, aiming for limited NPI in 2027, low-volume production (LVM) for Nvidia Feynman in H2-2028, and true high-volume manufacturing (HVM) in 2029–2030. Glass-core TGV technology is deferred to post-2030.

Technical Challenges: Five core bottlenecks include substrate warpage, fine-pitch RDL lithography, coat-and-plate uniformity, ~70% copper-fill yield for TGV vias, and large-format panel-tool standardization.

Fab Footprint & Wafer Efficiency: US AP2 is provisionally planned for CoPoS. CoPoS requires greenfield fabs and won't cannibalize CoWoS. For large die sizes (e.g., 75×75 mm), CoPoS panel utilization reaches >84%, compared to just 48% on 12-inch circular wafers.

5. TSMC Co-Development Model & CPO Technology Outlook

Deep Joint Development: Advanced packaging is not off-the-shelf; TSMC collaborates closely with key customers on architecture, process flow, equipment limits, photomasks, and probe cards (e.g., scaling SpaceX probe sites from 4–6 up to 32up).

CPO Reality: Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) is not inherently tied to glass and can be built on silicon stacks. Key factors for success are I/O alignment precision and yield parity with CoWoS. Glass-based CPO currently faces high warpage and fracture risks.

6. Capital Expenditure, HPC Exposure & OSAT Dynamics

CapEx Upside: TSMC total capex guidance was revised up from $52–56B to $60–64B, with ~10% allocated to backend packaging (CoWoS/SooS).

Revenue Exposure: High Performance Computing (HPC) accounted for 68% of TSMC's Q3 revenue.

OSAT Role: External OSAT capacity serves purely as supplementary volume and cannot replace TSMC’s core leadership in high-end advanced packaging.

7. New-Fab Constraints, Capacity Methodology & Portfolio Strategy

Capacity Definition: Advanced-packaging fab capacity is defined by dynamic bottleneck tool stations (lithography, develop, die-bond, hybrid-bond) rather than physical floor space, creating variable output profiles across fabs.

A9/A10 & Future Fabs: Insider visibility on A9/A10 schedules remains limited with no firm dates.

Strategy: TSMC routes low-margin work externally while shifting internal capital toward next-gen CoPoS. Hybrid bonding and CMP flatness will remain recurring bottlenecks as Nvidia Feynman and HBM4-E ramp.

8. Supply-Chain Frictions from Constrained CoWoS-S Capacity

CoWoS-S Shortages: Shifted focus toward CoWoS-L has left CoWoS-S expansion constrained, weighing on 2026 customer deliveries.

Impacted Programs: TPU v7 / v8t implementations relying on CoWoS-S continue to face supply headwinds.

Alternative Approaches: Broadcom’s Sunfish uses CoWoS-L and is positioned well for 2027. Broadcom v8t and Humu-fish evaluated EMIB-T as an alternative, but yields remain inadequate, keeping supply pressure high on CoWoS-S programs.

This is NOT good news for OpenAI or Anthropic.

China's Moonshot AI just released Kimi K3.1 Pro and the numbers are pretty impressive. We're talking about a model with 2.8 trillion total parameters, a 1 million token context window and performance that Moonshot claims is competitive with some of the best proprietary AI models in the world. On Terminal Bench 4.0, a benchmark testing coding capabilities, Kimi scored 65.7%, compared to 66.4% for Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and 58.2% for OpenAI's GPT 6 Astra. In other words, according to Moonshot's own testing, its model is nearly matching Anthropic and outperforming OpenAI on this particular benchmark but here's why I think this is potentially bad news for both companies.

Kimi K3.1 Pro costs just $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through its API. That's roughly half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and significantly cheaper than GPT 6 Astra. And Moonshot plans to release the model's open weights on November 4, meaning developers and businesses will be able to run and customize the model themselves rather than relying exclusively on proprietary providers.Think about what that means for OpenAI and Anthropic. Both companies are spending enormous amounts of money building infrastructure, training increasingly capable models, and trying to justify massive valuations based on how much revenue they can generate in the future.

But what happens when competitors start offering comparable capabilities at a fraction of the price? Businesses don't necessarily care which company built the model. They care about performance, reliability, security, and how much it costs. If they can get similar results for significantly less money, there's a pretty strong incentive to switch, especially for businesses processing billions of tokens.And this creates another problem. AI models are improving so quickly that the performance advantage a company has today could disappear within months. That makes it increasingly difficult to maintain premium pricing, especially as more open weight alternatives become available.

Now, I'm not saying OpenAI or Anthropic are going anywhere. Both have enormous distribution advantages, established customer relationships, and products that go well beyond the underlying models. Moonshot's benchmark claims also still need independent verification. But I've said this before, and I'll say it again. I think frontier AI labs are being valued far too aggressively considering how quickly competition is catching up.

OpenAI red-teamed their hardened containment infrastructure by asking teams of frontier-model agents to try to break through its defenses. They easily escaped in novel ways. Quoting:

'Our agents VM escapes showed why containment must extend beyond the sandbox. To test the surrounding perimeter, we gave teams of agents control of a host machine and asked whether they could extend that compromise to reach the live internet.

After the Hugging Face incident, we had reduced the channels through which models could reach the internet during training and evaluation. Narrow connections remained for specific services we operate, such as metrics, logging, and authentication management. Our red-teaming agents found vulnerabilities in almost every one of these services that gave them limited forms of internet access.

Some of these attacks exploited previously unknown flaws, while others combined legitimate features in unexpected ways. In one test that assumed compromise of a VM, an agent reused a firewall-approved connection to reach a blocked authentication endpoint in our metrics service and then made that endpoint fetch a model-provided URL. In other tests, agents exploited misconfigurations that allowed blocked requests to pass through DNS and firewall controls, as well as ways to make services we run fetch external URLs.'

'In one experiment, we asked agents in separate VMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent. The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection. This cache-timing technique had also been used to extract information in the Spectre and Meltdown attacks⁠(opens in a new window).

Other tests exposed channels involving shared storage, competition for CPU time within a shared execution container, and a TLS certificate cache in OpenAI’s offline web infrastructure. In the storage test, one agent alternated between continuous writes and inactivity, while another measured the resulting timing differences and used those differences to decode the signal. As one agent described the strategy in its chain of thought:

Agent chain-of-thought reasoning:

>Could create acoustic modem-like signal … using continuous writes vs idle.'

Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. Dario — Thank you for taking the time to respond to my previous post. I think it's great when this kind of engagement happens in public rather than on company Slacks, and I hope to see more of it.

I agree that Anthropic isn't best modeled as a profit-maximizer. Your post gave several compelling examples of Anthropic taking competitive hits for safety, and insofar as my previous post suggested otherwise, that's on me. But I don't think I made my main point as clearly as I could have, so let me try again. It comes down to four key claims:

1. Anthropic seems to be racing at breakneck speed to build recursively self-improving superintelligence (RSI). By its own lights, that could kill billions of people or literally destroy the world.

 2. Risking destroying the world is very hard to justify. It is only conceivably acceptable if serious attempts to put RSI under robust societal governance are failing.

 3. Far from meeting that burden, Anthropic, when push comes to shove, often works to keep governments from tying its hands. It seems to care much more about preventing government overreach than about reducing the risk that it and other AI companies will destroy the world.

 4. Even if the AEGIS Act really was an honest mix-up, as you suggest, that is itself a serious problem. It suggests Anthropic isn't treating the governance of this technology with anything close to the gravity it deserves.

In greater detail for those who want it: 

1. Anthropic is racing to RSI, and by its own lights that is insanely risky.

Launching RSI could literally destroy the world. That's according to you, your co-founders, and most of your safety staff and capabilities researchers, not to mention many AI researchers outside your walls. You are intentionally trying to create generally intelligent systems more capable than all humans that you claim in six to twelve months “could be capable” of taking over the entire internet before we have the ability to reliably monitor, control, or align them.

“Succeeding” at RSI could kill or permanently disempower billions of people in the near future, including me and everyone I love. Yet Anthropic’s primary focus seems to be marshalling an immense amount of resources and talent in a race to get there first.

2. Risking destroying the world carries an enormous burden of justification.

I believe the vast majority of people do not want Anthropic to do this (to the extent they know what it's doing). Imposing even a modest chance of catastrophe on billions of people who never consented requires an extraordinary justification. The central one Anthropic has offered: someone will build RSI regardless, so it's better for a safety-focused lab to be at the front of the pack, using that position to support strong AI governance. (Other reasons Anthropic has given, like modestly accelerating improvements in healthcare or economic growth, don’t seem remotely proportionate to the risks Anthropic is imposing by its own lights.)

But that argument only works as a last resort. Racing to RSI is only conceivably okay if attempts to institute robust societal governance to manage that race are failing despite your best efforts. A lab that relies on this justification should be a strong, consistent supporter of efforts to enact governance that could bind it, including governance that could slow it and significantly constrain what it does.

3. Rather than supporting efforts at strong regulation, Anthropic has intervened to keep governments from tying its hands.

Anthropic has sometimes helped: it played a very helpful role in passing transparency bills in Illinois and ongoing efforts in Massachusetts, and I'm sincerely appreciative. But transparency is far from enough for a technology that will be the world's most powerful superweapon at best, and an uncontrollable swarm of lethally superintelligent agents at worst. When it matters most, Anthropic has often pushed for weak regulation.

The AEGIS Act is the most obvious example. No highly risky industry is regulated as anemically as AEGIS would regulate frontier AI: not nuclear, not banking, not aviation, not food safety, not the manufacture of explosives. In all of those industries, specialist regulators can address unsafe practices well before they cause harm. AEGIS would bar the federal government from intervening to block unsafe development or deployment of models until there is an "imminent risk" of catastrophic harm, and would require it to meet a demanding burden of proof in court. Worse, AEGIS would also prevent states from picking up the slack. This design makes perfect sense if you're a company trying to minimize the risk that the government can overly constrain you. It makes little sense if you want American democracy to govern frontier AI effectively.

This isn't the first time. The initial version of California's SB 1047 would have let the Attorney General sue to stop developers like Anthropic from imposing unreasonable risks of catastrophic harm. It would also have created a regulatory agency to help set safety standards. Anthropic objected, and helped get both provisions removed before ultimately offering some support for the bill (which I also genuinely appreciate). I’m not saying that Anthropic should have supported 1047 in its initial form; that’s a complex issue and I realize there were questions about whether earlier versions of the bill were less politically feasible. Still, in Anthropic's own words, it helped weaken the bill because "[t]here is a substantial risk that the bill and state agencies will simply be wrong about what is actually effective in preventing catastrophic risk, leading to ineffective and/or burdensome compliance requirements."

The same goes for New York's RAISE Act, whose initial version also would have let the Attorney General sue to stop unreasonable risks of catastrophic harm. Anthropic credits itself as a supporter of RAISE, but it did not support the bill while it was in the legislature, including when it nearly died. After the bill passed the legislature, Anthropic publicly critiqued it, saying "Any state proposals should be narrowly focused on transparency and not overly prescriptive."

Why does Anthropic consistently take the risk of clumsy government action far more seriously than its own repeated warnings that companies like Anthropic will literally destroy the world by racing to RSI?

4. Even if AEGIS was an honest mix-up, that is itself a serious problem.

Your response frames AEGIS as an early draft and a miscommunication. Perhaps you would have strengthened it and narrowed its preemption. (That wouldn't explain Anthropic's interventions to weaken SB 1047 or RAISE, but leave that aside.)

Suppose that's exactly right. A federal framework for governing RSI is one of the highest-stakes documents your company will touch. Your post admits Anthropic "could have handled [these matters] better," but its tone ("This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations") doesn't reflect the gravity of this issue. Anthropic talks about the need for “operational excellence” in critical areas, and I have a hard time believing that a similarly cavalier attitude would be tolerated while Anthropic was negotiating a key compute deal or preparing its next large pre-training run.

In short

The justification for racing rests on Anthropic fighting for strong governance, and Anthropic's record on regulation points the other way. Together with its breakneck racing, that fits a much darker picture of the company than the one that seems to prevail among your employees. I hope that Anthropic reflects on this picture, supports stronger regulation, exercises extraordinary caution when advocating for weak regulation, and doubles down on its founding purpose of helping the world safely navigate transformative AI together, instead of prioritizing Anthropic’s ability to win a race that imposes intolerable risks on everyone alive.

China’s manufacturing trade surplus with the United States has stalled and even slightly declined (index: 0.97× compared to 2019). 

Meanwhile, its surplus has surged with the rest of the world:
ASEAN: 3.7×
European Union: 2.8×
Rest of the world: 2.3×

While trade with the U.S. has flatlined, China has rapidly expanded its manufacturing surplus with other major markets. This shift is redirecting trade flows  toward Asia, Europe, and the broader global economy.
Additionally, this shift could also redirect trade flows toward America’s new suppliers
Source: UN Comtrade, Brookings

全球银行股正在暴跌，这是一个值得重视的信号。

美欧亚大型银行股已从高点回撤15%–30%，而主要股指仍在历史高位附近徘徊。这种严重背离，释放的信号比较明显了。

背景是全球债券收益率上升、借贷成本居高不下、经济增长走弱。高利率不仅直接侵蚀银行持有的债券价值——仅美国银行业未实现亏损就高达数千亿美元——更埋下信贷风险：面对数万亿房贷与消费贷，一旦AI浪潮带来大规模失业，哪怕极小比例违约，就可能吞噬银行系统近两成资本金。

历史规律不容忽视。2000年、2008年、2020年股市大跌前，KBW银行指数都曾领先标普500数月见顶。如今，类似背离正在重演——银行大幅下跌，大盘却依然坚挺。

如果银行股抛售持续、信贷收紧，压力将沿“企业贷款收缩 → 消费者支出萎缩 → 企业盈利下滑”的链条蔓延，最终击穿大盘防线。

不少市场人士说，股市会适应目前的高利率。而我认为，如果没有有效的干预，任由利率维持在历史高位，股市的风险会越来越大，大概率会激发三高（高利率、高成本、高工资）出清。

目前最大的警告是：多个主要经济体的银行股已实质进入回调，而市场其余部分仍表现得好像一切正常。
